passage:
Before: When the unit test results came, Neelam got 71 in maths. Her friend Harish got 94 and said, "That was easy." At home, her mother asked what Harish got. Neelam lied and said 80. She went to bed feeling small and stupid.

During: The next week, a teacher asked the class to write one thing they had improved since last year. Neelam wrote: "I can do word problems now." It was true. She stared at the sentence for a while.

After: A few days later, she told her mother the real mark. Her mother was quiet, then asked, "Which part was hard?" They made a plan for algebra. Neelam still felt a pinch when Harish talked about marks, but it didn't stay all night.

qa.q: What mark did Neelam get in maths?
qa.a: She got 71.

qa.q: Why did Neelam lie about her mark?
qa.a: She was afraid of being compared with Harish and felt small and stupid, so she wanted to hide the gap from her mother.

qa.q: What helped Neelam's self-worth recover?
qa.a: Writing down a real improvement reminded her of her own progress, and her mother's focus on the hard part turned the talk into a plan instead of a judgement.

qa.q: What would change if her mother had scolded her for the real mark?
qa.a: Neelam might have kept lying and feeling small, and they would not have made a plan for algebra together.

grounding: It shows a teen coping over several days with rank comparison and parental expectations without losing self-worth.

passage: Manjula, sit with me. I want to tell you about your uncle Baljeet when he was your age. He came fifth in the district, and your grandfather asked, "Why not first?" I still remember his face. He stopped eating properly and studied every night till his eyes were red. One day he told me, "If I'm not first, I'm nothing." That scared me. So I took him to the fields where your grandfather grew up and asked him to help pick cotton for a day. He came back tired and laughing. That night, he said, "Bua, maybe fifth isn't nothing." He still worked hard. But he also played cricket again. Beta, marks matter. They're just not who you are.

qa.q: What rank did Baljeet get in the district?
qa.a: He came fifth in the district.

qa.q: What did Baljeet's words, "If I'm not first, I'm nothing," reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: They show he had tied his whole worth to his rank, which made him feel worthless despite doing well.

qa.q: What could Manjula take from Baljeet's story when feeling pressure?
qa.a: Manjula could keep working hard but also make room for enjoyable things, remembering that a mark does not decide anyone's value.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father have felt if he knew what his question caused?
qa.a: He might have felt sorry, since he likely meant to push Baljeet higher, not make him feel like nothing.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative about someone who coped with rank pressure without losing his sense of worth.

passage: The results went up on the board at nine, and by 9:05 Payal's phone was full of messages. "What did u get??" Her mother had already called twice. Payal had 82%. Her cousin Himani, who studied in the same school, had 91%. Payal's chest tightened. She went to the library, the only quiet place, and sat with her head on the desk. When her mother called a third time, she didn't pick up. Instead she wrote in her notebook: "82 is not a failure. I did better in physics than last year. I'm tired." Then she called back. "82, Ma. I know you hoped for more. I'm okay, and I'd like to talk tonight, not now." Her mother paused. "Okay. Come home, we'll eat."

qa.q: What percentage did Payal have?
qa.a: Payal had 82%.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she sat with her head on the desk?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, with a tight chest, because of the messages, her mother's calls and the comparison with Himani.

qa.q: What worked in the way Payal handled the pressure?
qa.a: She took a quiet moment, reminded herself of her progress in writing, then called back calmly and asked to talk later.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother have felt when Payal asked to talk later?
qa.a: She may have been disappointed but also reassured by Payal's calm voice, and chose to support her by inviting her home to eat.

grounding: It shows a teen under results-day pressure coping with rank comparison and parental expectations while keeping her self-worth.

passage: Harsha's mock test rank came on the coaching centre board in Hyderabad: 312. Last month it had been 48. She stood on the stairs, stomach empty, while other students pushed past. At home, Nanna said, 'Your cousin Sanjay stayed in the top fifty,' and went back to his phone. Harsha went to her room and stared at the ceiling. 'Maybe I'm just stupid.' Her sister Gargi came in with two cups of tea. 'One test. Which section dropped?' 'Chemistry.' 'Only chemistry?' Harsha checked. It was. Gargi said, 'So you're not stupid. You have a chemistry problem.' Harsha laughed a little. Later, she knocked on Nanna's door. 'Nanna, when you compare me to Sanjay, it makes me want to give up. Can you just ask me what went wrong?'

qa.q: What was Harsha's rank this month, and what had it been last month?
qa.a: It was 312 this month, and it had been 48 last month.

qa.q: What does Harsha saying 'Maybe I'm just stupid' reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: She was letting one bad rank make her doubt her whole worth, feeling hopeless after the comparison.

qa.q: How did Gargi help without dismissing Harsha's worry?
qa.a: She asked which section dropped, which turned a crushing rank into one specific problem Harsha could work on.

qa.q: How might Nanna feel when Harsha asks him not to compare her?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or a little defensive at first, but it gives him a chance to support her better.

grounding: Shows a teen coping with a rank drop and parental comparison without losing her self-worth.

passage: 'Papa, results are out.' Anand looked up from the laptop. 'And?' 'Seventy-eight percent.' 'Hmm. Mehta's daughter got ninety-two.' Disha's face went still. 'Can you not? Just once?' 'I'm only saying, beta, you're capable of more.' 'I know I'm capable! I studied every day for three months. I got stuck on maths. I'm still proud of English.' Anand closed the laptop. 'I didn't know about maths.' 'Because you only asked about marks.' Silence. 'What was hard?' 'Probability. I panicked.' 'We'll find a tutor for that, if you want. And English? Show me.' She handed over the marksheet. 'Ninety-one.' He smiled for the first time. 'Better than Mehta's daughter.' 'Papa!' 'Sorry, sorry. Better than last year.'

qa.q: What percentage did Disha get overall?
qa.a: She got seventy-eight percent.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when Papa mentioned Mehta's daughter?
qa.a: She was hurt and frustrated, her face going still, because she had worked hard and felt compared again.

qa.q: What turned the conversation around?
qa.a: Papa closed the laptop and asked what was hard, so they could focus on her effort and a real plan for maths.

qa.q: What might Papa realise from Disha's 'Because you only asked about marks'?
qa.a: He might realise his focus on marks and comparisons made her hide her struggles from him.

grounding: Shows a teen coping with marks and parental comparison and keeping her self-worth through honest talk.

passage:
When the Class 10 results came, I was fourth in my class. I'm Seema. I'd been first for three years.
At dinner, my father Shankar looked at the report card for a long time. Then he said, “What happened?” I went to my room without eating.
That night I lay awake thinking I was a failure. Fourth. As if the number was all of me.
The next morning Papa knocked. He sat on my bed. “I was wrong last night. I asked the wrong question. I should've asked how you are.”
I cried. I told him how tired I'd been, how scared of not being first.
He said, “You're my daughter, not your rank.”
I still want to do well. But I'm learning the number isn't me.

qa.q: What rank did Seema get in Class 10?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Seema feel on the night of the results?
qa.a: She felt worthless and ashamed, like a failure, as if her rank was all of her.

qa.q: What did Shankar do the next morning that helped?
qa.a: He admitted he asked the wrong question, asked how Seema was, and said she was more than her rank.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt after seeing Seema's reaction?
qa.a: He probably felt regretful and worried, realising his words had hurt her.

grounding: A teenager learns, with her father's apology, that her rank does not define her worth.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11. Tanvir Ahmed.
Mridul (sixteen), usually first in class, came ninth in the mid-term exams. This week he stopped eating lunch and sat alone. Today, when I returned his paper, he said quietly, “I'm useless. My parents will be so disappointed.”
I took the words seriously. At break I sat with him in the empty classroom. I told him one exam does not measure his worth, and asked how he was really feeling. He said he couldn't sleep.
The same afternoon I took him to the school counsellor, Ms Mehta, who spoke with him and then called his parents. They came in after school.
Next step: weekly check-ins with Mridul and a class talk on rank pressure.

qa.q: What rank did Mridul get in the mid-term exams?
qa.a: Ninth.

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling after the results?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and worthless, calling himself useless and not sleeping.

qa.q: What did the teacher do right when Mridul said he was useless?
qa.a: He took it seriously, talked with Mridul, took him to the counsellor and involved his parents the same day.

qa.q: How might Mridul's parents feel when they are called to school?
qa.a: They may feel worried but grateful the school noticed, and want to support him.

grounding: A teacher responds the same day to a sixteen-year-old struggling with rank and self-worth.

passage:
Sunday night
Family lunch today. Deepika-didi got 98% in the boards and everyone kept saying it. Dadi looked at me and said, “And you, Darshan? You'll do the same next year, na?”
I nodded and ate my rice very slowly.
Later, Deepika found me on the terrace. I thought she'd brag. Instead she said, “Everyone thinks I was calm. I cried every night for two months.”
I didn't know that.
She said, “Don't try to be me. Just do your best and tell someone when it's too much.”
I told her I'm scared of disappointing everyone. She said she was too.
I'm still scared. But now I know I'm not the only one. — Darshan

qa.q: What did Deepika-didi get in the boards?
How did Darshan feel when Dadi asked about next year?
qa.a: Darshan felt pressured and anxious, eating very slowly.

qa.q: What did Deepika say that helped Darshan?
qa.a: That she had cried every night too, and that Darshan should do their best and tell someone when it's too much.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel after talking to Darshan on the terrace?
qa.a: She probably feels close to Darshan and glad she shared her own struggle.

grounding: A teenager copes with family comparison after a cousin shares her own exam pressure.

passage:
In the kasba, everyone compared Rukmini with her cousin Shalini. Shalini always came first. Rukmini came somewhere in the middle.
At the family dinner after results, her uncle said, "Shalini got 96. Rukmini, what happened?"
Rukmini stared at her plate. Her ears burned.
Shalini put down her spoon. "Rukmini made the best science model in the district. She did that alone."
Everyone went quiet.
Later, on the terrace, Rukmini said, "Thanks. But I still feel like the second one."
Shalini shrugged. "I'm scared all the time of not coming first. It's not fun either."
They sat in silence. Rukmini realised: nobody at the top was feeling great either.

qa.q: What did Shalini say Rukmini made?
qa.a: The best science model in the district.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when her ears burned?
qa.a: Rukmini felt humiliated and small at being compared to Shalini in front of family.

qa.q: How did Shalini help, and what else could help Rukmini?
qa.a: Shalini named Rukmini's real strength; Rukmini could also focus on her own progress rather than ranks.

qa.q: How does Shalini see coming first?
qa.a: Shalini feels constant fear of not coming first, so being top isn't as happy as it looks.

grounding: A teen in a small town faces rank comparison and learns her cousin also struggles with pressure.

passage:
In Warsaw, the school posted everyone's rank online. Marek was 27th out of 30. His phone buzzed with messages: "How'd you do?"
He didn't answer. At home, he lay on his bed and stared at the ceiling.
Bao, his friend, came over with a bag of chips. "I saw. I'm 19th. Want to be sad together?"
Marek laughed despite himself. "My mum will be so disappointed."
"Did you try?"
"Yes. Maths was a disaster."
"Then that's the problem to fix. Not you."
They opened his maths paper. Bao pointed at three mistakes. "Same kind. You can learn this."
That evening, Marek told his mum, "I'll ask for extra help in maths." She hugged him.

qa.q: What rank was Marek?
qa.a: 27th out of 30.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling as he stared at the ceiling?
qa.a: Marek felt ashamed and dreaded his mum's disappointment.

qa.q: What did Bao do that helped Marek move forward?
qa.a: Bao separated the problem from Marek himself and helped him spot a pattern in his mistakes.

qa.q: How might Marek's mum feel when he tells her his plan?
qa.a: His mum probably feels relieved and proud that he has a plan, which is why she hugs him.

grounding: A teen in Poland copes with a low rank and focuses on fixing specific gaps.

passage:
The coaching centre pinned the weekly rank list outside the office. Kishore saw his name at 43. Last month he'd been 12. He went to the back staircase and sat with his head on his knees.
Vidya Ma'am, the centre's counsellor, found him there. She sat two steps below. "The list?"
He nodded. "Papa will ask. He always asks."
"What happened this week?"
He explained: a fever on Tuesday, then he rushed the physics test.
"So a rank tells us about one test in one bad week. It doesn't tell us who you are."
He didn't believe her, not fully. But she helped him write down what he'd do differently and offered to call his father with him that evening. He said yes. His father's voice on speaker was calmer than he'd feared.

qa.q: What rank did Kishore see next to his name?
qa.a: Kishore saw his name at 43.

qa.q: Why did Kishore sit with his head on his knees?
qa.a: Kishore felt crushed and anxious about the drop, and dreaded his father asking about it.

qa.q: How did Vidya Ma'am help without dismissing his worry?
qa.a: She asked what happened, separated one bad week from who he is, helped him plan and offered to call his father with him.

qa.q: How might Kishore's father have seen the call?
qa.a: Hearing the reasons and the plan with the counsellor there, his father may have felt more understanding than angry.

grounding: Illustrates a teen coping with a rank drop and parental expectation with a counsellor's support that protects his self-worth.

passage:
Dear Shreya Didi,
You're lucky you're in college and don't have to hear it anymore. Every time Mama's cousin calls, it's "What did Lalit get? Rohit got 96." Then Mama goes quiet for the whole evening, and I feel like a disappointment.
I got 81 in the half-yearly. I actually worked hard. But nobody says anything about that.
Last week I stopped sleeping properly. I kept doing sums in my head at night. Then I remembered what you told me in the summer: "Marks are information, not a verdict." So I made a list: things I'm good at that aren't on the report card. Fixing the neighbours' fans. Explaining maths to Pintu. It helped a little.
I also told Mama how the calls make me feel. She hugged me. She said she'll stop answering on speaker.
Write back?
Lalit

qa.q: What marks did Lalit get in the half-yearly?
qa.a: Lalit got 81.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel when Mama goes quiet after the cousin's calls?
qa.a: Lalit feels like a disappointment and anxious enough that sleep became hard.

qa.q: Which of Lalit's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mama how the calls felt helped most, because it changed what happened at home, while the list helped Lalit remember Lalit's own worth.

qa.q: How might Mama feel after Lalit tells her?
qa.a: Mama probably felt sorry and protective, not having realised how the comparisons were hurting Lalit.

grounding: Shows a teen coping with comparison and parental expectations by holding onto self-worth and speaking up.

passage:
Rekha, you asked on the podcast what Class 10 was like for me. Okay. I'm Sonali, and it was bad.
My parents are both doctors. Everyone assumed I'd be one too. Every test, I'd check the rank list before I checked my own answers. Rank 5 felt like failing because rank 1 existed.
One day I got a 12 out of 20 in chemistry and I couldn't stop crying in the school washroom. My friend found me and walked me to our class teacher, who called my mother right away. My mother left the hospital and came. She held my hands in the car and said, "I never needed you to be first. I needed you to be okay." I didn't know that. I'd never asked.
After that we talked properly. I still care about marks. But now I ask what I learned, not where I stand.

qa.q: What mark did Sonali get in chemistry that day?
qa.a: Sonali got 12 out of 20 in chemistry.

qa.q: Why did rank 5 feel like failing to Sonali?
qa.a: Sonali felt anxious and inadequate because Sonali was measured against rank 1 and against the parents' expected path.

qa.q: What turned things around for Sonali, and what could others learn?
qa.a: A friend and teacher bringing in Sonali's mother, and then an honest talk, showed Sonali the expectations were partly assumptions; others can ask their parents directly.

qa.q: How might Sonali's mother have felt in the car?
qa.a: Sonali's mother was probably shocked and sad that Sonali had carried so much pressure, and deeply relieved to be told.

grounding: Illustrates a teen's rank anxiety and how an honest conversation with a parent restored the teen's self-worth.

passage:
I'm Pankaj, and I sit behind Jahnavi in Class 11. When the mock test ranks came out, she dropped from third to nineteenth. She stared at the list, then folded it very small and put it in her pocket.
At lunch she didn't eat. She said, "Papa will ask who came first. He always does."
A week later, she wasn't laughing in class anymore. I told our class teacher I was worried about her. The teacher called her in that afternoon and asked the school counsellor to join. I don't know what they talked about.
But the next Monday, Jahnavi said, "The counsellor asked me what I actually got wrong. It was mostly one chapter." She'd made a plan for it. She also said her mother came to meet the counsellor too.
She's still nervous before tests. But she's eating lunch again.

qa.q: What rank did Jahnavi drop to?
qa.a: She dropped from third to nineteenth.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi folding the list very small suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed and anxious, wanting to hide her rank and dreading her father's question.

qa.q: What small step helped Jahnavi cope with the rank?
qa.a: Looking with the counsellor at what she actually got wrong showed it was mostly one chapter, so she could make a plan instead of feeling like a failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Pankaj to watch Jahnavi change?
qa.a: Pankaj was worried enough to tell the class teacher, and now seems relieved to see her eating lunch again.

grounding: Shows a teenager coping with rank pressure and parental expectations with support from a teacher and counsellor.
